DispatchThe dispatcher is one loop

    

      
for(;;){

      
  sti();                      // allow interrupts

      
  acquire(&ptable.lock);

      
  for(p = ptable.proc; p < &ptable.proc[NPROC]; p++){

      
    if(p->state != RUNNABLE)

      
      continue;

      
    c->proc = p;

      
    switchuvm(p);              // its page table

      
    p->state = RUNNING;

      
    swtch(&(c->scheduler), p->context);   // run it

      
    switchkvm();               // it gave the CPU back

      
    c->proc = 0;

      
  }

      
  release(&ptable.lock);

      
}

DispatchHow does the CPU come back?

    

    

      
// trap.c: Force process to give up CPU on clock tick.

      
if(myproc() && myproc()->state == RUNNING &&

      
   tf->trapno == T_IRQ0+IRQ_TIMER)

      
  yield();

      
void yield(void) {

      
  acquire(&ptable.lock);

      
  myproc()->state = RUNNABLE;

      
  sched();                   // back to the scheduler loop

      
  release(&ptable.lock);

      
}

DispatchA context switch in 13 instructions

    

      
# void swtch(struct context **old,

      
#            struct context *new);

      
swtch:

      
  movl 4(%esp), %eax   # old

      
  movl 8(%esp), %edx   # new

      
  pushl %ebp

      
  pushl %ebx

      
  pushl %esi

      
  pushl %edi

      
  movl %esp, (%eax)

      
  movl %edx, %esp

      
  popl %edi

      
  popl %esi

      
  popl %ebx

      
  popl %ebp

      
  ret

Amdahl's lawMore cores: how much faster?

    

      
def speedup(P, N):

      
    serial = 1 - P          # runs on one core

      
    parallel = P / N        # split across N cores

      
    return 1 / (serial + parallel)

    

    
speedup = 1 / ( (1 − P) + P / N )

    
P = 0.75 of the work can run in parallel

    
Gene AmdahlAFIPS 1967

    

    
python3 amdahl.py

    
With 25% serial work, no number of cores gives more than 4x

PoliciesShortest job first: 110 becomes 50

    

      
fifo  = lambda r, j, l: min(r, key=lambda n: j[n][0])   # earliest arrival

      
short = lambda r, j, l: min(r, key=lambda n: l[n])      # least work left

      
step = min(left[n], min(nxt) - t) if preempt and nxt else left[n]   # STCF: stop at the next arrival

    

    

    
But who knows how long a job will run?and a stream of short jobs can starve a long one

    
Short jobs first gives the best average turnaround, if you know the future

PoliciesRound robin, one slice per click

    

      
admit(t)

      
while ready or todo:

      
    job = ready.popleft()            # take the job at the head

      
    run = min(Q, left[job])          # one slice, or less

      
    t += run; left[job] -= run

      
    admit(t)                         # new arrivals join first

      
    if left[job]:

      
        ready.append(job)            # unfinished: back of the queue

PoliciesMLFQ: learn from how a job behaves

    

      
top = next(i for i in range(3) if Q[i])

      
if cur and top < level[cur]:            # rule 1: higher queue preempts

      
    Q[level[cur]].appendleft(cur); cur = None

      
if cur is None:

      
    cur, used = Q[top].popleft(), 0     # rule 2: round robin in a level

      
work[j] -= 1; used += 1

      
if j == 'B':                            # rule 4b: gave up the CPU early,

      
    back[j] = t + 3                     #   stays at its level

      
elif used == SLICE[lv]:                 # rule 4a: used the whole slice,

      
    level[j] = min(lv + 1, 2)           #   moves down one level

PoliciesLottery: tickets buy a share of the CPU

    

      
node_t *draw(int winner) {

      
    int counter = 0;           // tickets seen so far

      
    node_t *current = head;    // walk the list of jobs

      
    while (current) {

      
        counter = counter + current->tickets;

      
        if (counter > winner)

      
            break;             // found the winner

      
        current = current->next;

      
    }

      
    return current;            // schedule it

      
}
